newsitem.title: USA: Capitol Hill and business decry Fed rate hikes.
newsitem.headline: Capitol Hill and business decry Fed rate hikes.

text.p: The Federal Reserve was deluged with criticism Tuesday following a decision by policy-makers to raise interest rates for the first time in more than two years.

From the business community to Capitol Hill, there were no apparent early defenders of the quarter-percentage-point increase by the Fed on the grounds that it needed to stay in front of any inflation threat.
"The Fed does not have the right to be wrong when every American citizen is forced to pay for their mistakes," said Sen. Byron Dorgan, a North Dakota Democrat.

Only the Clinton administration was generally muted in its reaction, saying the administration respected the Fed's independence and remained confident the economy would continue to grow as it entered the seventh year of expansion.
Joint Economic Committee Chairman Jim Saxton, a Republican representative from New Jersey, said that if the Fed did feel the need to act, he hoped it would stop at just one move.

The Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee raised the federal funds rate that banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.50 percent but left the discount rate it charges banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.
"The fact that the Federal Reserve did not raise the discount rate along with the federal funds rate suggests that this move may not be a prelude to a string of additional rate hikes," Saxton said.
The business community also was less than pleased. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce strongly argued that, with little inflation to worry about, the Fed could have waited longer before acting.
"Clearly, the pressure to raise rates came from the brokerage houses on Wall Street, not the small businesses on Main Street," said Chamber of Commerce chief economist Martin Regalia.
The business group said that since the financial markets have already raised rates in anticipation of the Fed's move, its action will have only a modest impact on economic activity.
"However, if this is merely a first step in a replay of 1994, economic growth will be noticeably impacted," the chamber warned.
The National Association of Manufacturers called the Fed action regrettable and a serious mistake.
"The Federal Reserve's decision to raise interest rates was simply wrong. It will impede economic growth and make life tougher on consumers and job-creating businesses," it said.
Sen. Paul Sarbanes said that even without any further action, the Fed increase would take a painful slice out of economic activity and was without justification.
"This is a pre-emptive strike against economic growth and against jobs," the Maryland Democrat told reporters.
